entries.narration: Shopwave is an online store, and every order it takes lands in one place: the shop's PostgreSQL database. The explorer shows that database's schema and the script that loads Shopwave's year into it, all twenty twenty six, from a seeded generator, so every number on screen is one a real run printed. Now the finance team asks a simple question: how much revenue did each category make, month by month? The editor holds the answer, in plain S Q L. Look at the side pane to see what that one question needs. A category lives on the product, a date and a status live on the order, and the money lives on the order line, so the query joins three tables by their keys, for every line of the year, and then groups them by month. It also has to spell out every category as its own column, because the shop's schema knows orders, not categories by month. The terminal shows the result, twelve months by six categories, and the chart at the bottom of the side pane adds each month up: November towers over the rest, because Black Friday is in it. It works. But this database was built for something else: taking one order at a time, inserting it, updating it, finding it by its key, quickly, while customers wait. A question over the whole year reads every line, and when every analyst asks one every month, they ask it on the same server that takes the orders. The next section looks at why the shape of the storage itself is the problem.

Two kinds of database answer two kinds of question. O L T P, online transaction processing, is the shop: one order at a time. O L A P, online analytical processing, is the warehouse: all the orders at once. The difference starts with how the rows are stored, so this lab stores Shopwave's order lines for the year twice and measures what each layout must read. On the left, by row, as the shop database stores them: each order line's values sit together. Fetching one order reads only its lines, a few dozen bytes, side by side. But revenue for the year needs two columns, quantity and unit price, and a row store must read every column of every row to get them. In the middle, by column, as a warehouse stores them: each column's values sit together, compressed. Revenue now reads just those two columns, a small fraction of the bytes. The price moves to the other question: one order means fetching a piece of every column and putting the row back together. Underneath, the file itself, column by column: what each one costs to read. And on the right, the lab's own output. The same split runs through how the data is modelled. The shop's schema is normalised: each fact stored once, many tables, joined for each question. A warehouse's is dimensional: facts at a declared grain, with dimensions around them, built for exactly these questions. Snowflake is a column store, and that is the warehouse we will build.

This is the warehouse we will build, from an empty Snowflake account to the end of the course. On the left are Shopwave's sources: the shop database, a payment provider's daily Parquet files, the website's clicks as JSON, returns from the warehouse in an old encoding, and exchange rates for four currencies. In the middle is one Snowflake account, and the data flows through it left to right. Files land in a stage and load into the raw database exactly as they came, never edited. Staging models clean, rename and type them, and snapshots keep the history of customers and prices. The marts hold the dimensional model: a star with order lines at its centre, and more facts for the order lifecycle, returns, sessions and the funnel. And the B I layer holds one definition of revenue that every dashboard shares. Underneath runs everything that keeps it working: three warehouses that bill only while they run, under a monthly budget; roles that let each team in only as far as it needs, with key pairs for the services and policies that mask personal data; and d b t to build and test it all, tasks to run it every night, and a clone to change it safely. On the right are the readers: finance's dashboard, analysts with their own S Q L, and Brightline, the marketing agency, reading a secure share without a copy. Each course adds parts to this map. First, how Snowflake itself is built.

Before we load anything, let's look at how Snowflake is built, because it explains how you pay for it. Snowflake is three layers, and each one scales on its own. At the top is cloud services. It is always on, and it is the part you talk to: it logs you in, checks your role, parses and optimises every query, and keeps the metadata about every table. In the middle is compute: virtual warehouses. A warehouse is a cluster of servers that runs the heavy part of a query, and it is billed per second, only while it runs. You can have many, one per team, and none of them slows another down. At the bottom is storage. Every table lives in cloud object storage, here on A W S in Northern Virginia, as compressed, columnar files, and storage is billed by the terabyte, whether or not any warehouse is running. The terminal on the right is a new trial account, asked four questions. Its version. Which warehouses exist: only the ones Snowflake makes for every trial, one of them, compute W H, running because the trial's own setup uses it. Which databases exist: Snowflake's own, a sample database shared into every account, and a personal one for the user. And how many orders are in one of the sample tables. Listing objects and counting a table's rows are questions about metadata, so cloud services can answer them alone, without needing a warehouse at all. Separate layers mean separate bills: you pay for compute only when you use it. So the next question is what a warehouse is, and what it costs.

Shopwave's first warehouse is for loading data, so it is called W H underscore LOAD. The editor creates it with four settings, and each one is about money. The size is extra small, the smallest there is. Auto suspend is sixty seconds: after a minute with nothing to do, it stops. Auto resume is on, so the next query that needs it starts it again. And it is created suspended, so it costs nothing until someone uses it. The terminal runs the file, then a second one that sets W H LOAD as the session's warehouse, shows its state, runs a query that really computes, a sum over a sample table, and shows its state again. Look at the side pane to follow that. A warehouse spends its life suspended, costing nothing. A query arrives, it resumes, and billing starts, per second, with a sixty second minimum every time it starts. When the work is done it stays up for its auto suspend time, and that idle minute is billed too, then it suspends again. What it costs per second is set by its size. Snowflake bills in credits, and an extra small warehouse uses one credit per hour of running. Every size up doubles the servers and doubles the rate: small is two, medium four, large eight. Twice the size often finishes in half the time, so a bigger warehouse is not always a dearer one. Before we choose sizes, though, we need to see what a warehouse actually reads.

Everything a warehouse reads is stored the same way, in micro-partitions, and they explain most of how Snowflake performs. To see them, this step copies one of the sample tables, the T P C H line item table, into a table of our own, measures it, and drops it again. The terminal shows the copy, then two questions about the result. How many rows, and how many bytes they take once stored. And how Snowflake split them. Look at the left of the frame. When a table is loaded, Snowflake cuts it into micro-partitions: small files, each holding between fifty and five hundred megabytes of data before compression, and each one columnar inside, every column stored and compressed apart, the way the first course's lab measured. A micro-partition is immutable. Snowflake never edits one in place: an update writes new partitions and retires the old ones, which is also what makes time travel and cloning possible later in the course. For every partition, cloud services keeps metadata: among other things, the minimum and maximum of every column. That is what lets a query skip partitions it does not need. Ask for one day of shipping dates, and every partition whose range of dates cannot contain that day is never read. The last number is the clustering depth on the ship date: roughly, how many partitions overlap at any one date. In this run there are eight partitions and the depth is eight: every partition holds every ship date, because the rows were stored in the order they arrived, not by date. So a query for one day of shipping could skip none of them. Low depth means good skipping, and course ten shows how to get it, on Shopwave's own data. Next: where an account lives.

Every Snowflake account lives somewhere, and the query in the editor asks where. Four functions: the organisation, the account's name, its locator, and its region. The terminal shows the answers, and the side pane draws them. At the top is the organisation, which is the company. It owns the accounts, and it is where billing and contracts live. Shopwave has one account today. A bigger company might have one for production, one for development, and one in another region, all under one organisation. Each account runs in exactly one cloud and one region, here A W S in Northern Virginia, in the United States, which matters for two reasons: your data stays in that region, and moving data to an account in another region costs transfer fees. A European shop like Shopwave would normally choose a European region for its customers' data; this course's trial account happens to run in the United States. An account has two names. The modern one is the organisation name and the account name, joined by a hyphen, and that is what the connection on this machine uses, and what you will see in every web address. The older one is the locator, a short code tied to the region, which some tools and older documentation still ask for. One thing on screen is not quite what Snowflake printed. The real names of the trial account behind this course are replaced, as it is recorded, with the names Shopwave uses, so no real account identifier ever appears in a frame. The shape of the answer is real; only the names are swapped. Next, what each edition of Snowflake adds, and why this course needs Enterprise.

Snowflake comes in editions, and each one includes everything in the one before it. This frame is drawn from Snowflake's documentation, not from a run. Standard is the base: virtual warehouses, resource monitors to cap spending, network policies and single sign on, and time travel that can look back one day. Shopwave's warehouse uses all of these. Enterprise adds what makes a warehouse fast at scale and safe to share. Multi cluster warehouses, which add clusters when too many people query at once, used in course ten for Black Friday. Materialised views, search optimisation and query acceleration, three more ways to make queries faster, also in course ten. Masking policies and row access policies, which decide what each reader sees, column by column and row by row, in course eleven. And time travel up to ninety days. The tinted features are the ones this course uses, which is why the trial behind it is an Enterprise account. Business Critical adds what regulated companies need: encryption with a key the customer holds, called Tri Secret Secure, private network connections to Snowflake, failover between accounts in different regions, and support for health data. And Virtual Private Snowflake gives a company its own metadata store and compute, sharing no hardware with any other account. Editions change the price of a credit, not how credits are counted, so everything we learn about cost holds in every edition. Next, the different ways to reach the same service.

There are many ways to talk to Snowflake, and they all reach the same place. The terminal asks the same question twice. First the Snowflake command line, snow, which this course uses everywhere: it prints its version, then asks Snowflake which client it is talking to. Then the editor's small Python program, which connects with the Snowflake connector for Python, using the same saved connection, and asks the same thing. Each answer names the driver that sent the query and its version. Look at the side pane. There are three kinds of client on the top row. Snowsight is Snowflake's web interface, where most people start: worksheets, charts and the account's settings in a browser. This course never shows it, because everything it does can be done in S Q L, and a terminal is something we can record and replay. The command line is a Python program, and under the hood it is built on that very Python connector. And the connector is how programs talk to Snowflake: there are equivalents for Java, Go, Node and others. Whatever the client, the request lands at cloud services. It logs the user in, checks the role, plans the query, and only then, if the query needs to compute, hands it to a warehouse. That is why a client never chooses where data lives or how it is read: it only sends S Q L. Which leaves one question for this course: what all of that costs.

Before Shopwave opens its warehouse, it wants to know what a day will cost, so this lab builds a model. To be clear about what it is: it applies Snowflake's published billing rules to a day Shopwave plans to have. It runs on this machine, and it proves nothing about Snowflake itself. The rules are written in the file's opening lines: credits per hour by size, per second billing with a sixty second minimum each time a warehouse starts, and auto suspend. The editor shows what comes after them. First the day: a nightly load, a d b t build after it, and a dashboard that refreshes every fifteen minutes through the working day, each refresh a three second query. Then the billing function, which walks the queries in order: a query that arrives while the warehouse is still up joins the same run; any other starts a new one, billed at least a minute. The terminal shows the result. The load and the build cost little, because they work for minutes at a time. The dashboard is the surprise. Its queries work for about two minutes in a whole day, yet it is billed for nearly an hour, because each three second query costs a resume, the sixty second minimum, and the idle minute before it suspends. The side pane draws one of those queries, and the table under it shows the day. With auto suspend at ten minutes, the same dashboard costs about ten times as much. A busy dashboard can share a warehouse that stays awake; a quiet one should be left to sleep. With that, the account can be opened.

Shopwave's warehouse starts where its data starts: the shop's own database. It runs on PostgreSQL, on this machine, holding the shop's whole year, twenty twenty six, from the same seeded generator as every other step. The explorer shows the two scripts that create it and load it, and the editor holds one query that asks each table how many rows it has and how much space it takes. The terminal shows four tables. Orders, one row per order, about twenty thousand of them at the scale this course uses. Order items, one row per line of an order. Customers, and products. Look at the side pane to see how they fit together. This is a normalised schema, the shape every shop database has. Each fact is stored once: an order points at its customer by the customer's id, and each order line points at its order and at its product by theirs. That is exactly right for taking orders, and it is why the first course's question needed three joins. The table underneath is the plan for these four tables: they will all be copied into Snowflake, into a database called raw, exactly as they are. Products go first, in this course, because they are small and change rarely; the rest arrive in course five, with the files from the payment provider, the website and the warehouse. The shop itself keeps running on PostgreSQL. The warehouse never replaces it, it only copies from it. Next, the places in Snowflake those copies will go.

Everything in Snowflake lives in a database, and every database is divided into schemas. The editor creates the two databases Shopwave's warehouse will use, and the names say what each is for. Raw holds the sources exactly as they arrive, never edited, so that anything built later can always be rebuilt from it. It has one schema, Shopwave, for the shop's data. Analytics holds what we make of it, in three schemas that match the layers of the warehouse: staging, for cleaned and renamed copies of each source; marts, for the dimensional model; and B I, for what dashboards read. Snowflake creates a schema called public in every new database; the file drops both, so nothing ends up somewhere nobody meant. Look at the side pane to see the hierarchy. The account holds databases, a database holds schemas, and a schema holds the objects: tables, views, stages, file formats, and more. Every object has a three part name, database, schema, object, like raw dot Shopwave dot products, so a query can say exactly what it means, from any database. The last statement in the file asks Snowflake for every schema in the two new databases, and the terminal shows the answer. None of this needed a warehouse: creating a database or a schema is metadata, handled by cloud services, and costs nothing until data arrives. A database with nothing in it teaches nothing, though, so next we load a first table.

Shopwave's first table in Snowflake is its products, small enough to load by hand. The terminal does it in four steps. First it makes a folder for exports, then asks PostgreSQL to copy the products table out to a C S V file. Then it runs the file in the editor. It sets the warehouse and the schema, and creates a table with the same columns as the shop's, in Snowflake's types. Then it puts the file into the table's own stage: every table in Snowflake has one, a small place for files on their way in, written with a percent sign. Course five builds a proper stage for every source; this one is enough for a single file. Finally, copy into loads the file's rows into the table, skipping the header. The last command asks the first question of the warehouse: how many products there are in each category, and their average price. Look at the side pane to follow that question's round trip, because every query in this course takes the same one. The client sends the S Q L. Cloud services parses and plans it. The warehouse, W H LOAD, resumes and does the work, reading the table's micro-partitions from storage, and the answer travels back. A minute later, with nothing more to do, the warehouse suspends again. Under the trip is the answer itself, as Snowflake returned it. One question does not tell us much about the warehouse's size, though, so next we ask a bigger one, twice.

How big should a warehouse be? This step measures it. The editor runs one query twice over a large sample table, six hundred million order lines, first on W H LOAD at extra small, then again after resizing it to small. The result cache is switched off for the session, so each run really reads the data, and each run is tagged, so the last query can find both in the session's query history and show how long each took. Look at the side pane. The table compares the two runs: small costs two credits an hour instead of one, and the elapsed times say what that bought. When a query reads a lot of data, doubling the warehouse often roughly halves the time, which means it costs about the same and answers sooner. When a query is small, a bigger warehouse just costs more. Times vary from run to run, so the numbers on screen are this run's, not a promise. The file puts the warehouse back to extra small, because that is what loading needs. Then the terminal does something unusual: it waits. It shows the warehouse's state, sleeps for a minute and a half, and shows it again. The diagram follows the warehouse through the step: resumed for the first query, resized and resized back, then idle for its sixty second auto suspend, and finally suspended by itself, costing nothing. Auto suspend is the setting that saves the most money. But it stops nobody from spending: for that, the warehouse needs a budget.

A trial account has a fixed number of credits, and a real company has a budget, so Shopwave's warehouse gets one before anything else is loaded. The editor creates a resource monitor called R M monthly. It allows fifty credits a month, starting today. It has two triggers. At eighty percent, forty credits, it notifies the account's administrators by email. At a hundred percent, fifty credits, it suspends every warehouse it watches: queries already running are allowed to finish, and nothing new starts until the next month, or until an administrator raises the limit. Then the file attaches the monitor to W H LOAD, and asks for both, so the terminal shows the monitor's quota and credits used so far, and the warehouse with its monitor. Look at the side pane. One monitor can watch many warehouses. Today there is one; W H transform arrives with d b t in course seven, and W H B I for the analysts in the next course, and both will be attached to the same monitor, shown dashed until they exist. The table under it is what happens as credits are used. One more line in the file deserves a note. A resource monitor can only be created by the account administrator role, so the file switches to it for this. Using the most powerful role for everyday work is a habit to avoid, and the next course is about roles. First, one more thing that makes queries cheaper: caching.

Why does the same query sometimes cost nothing the second time? Snowflake has three caches, and this step shows each. It first shows the warehouse suspended, idle since the last step, so nothing is cached on it, then switches off the result cache for the session and runs one query over the sample order lines. That is the cold run: every micro-partition it needs is read from storage. Then it runs the same query again. The warehouse is still up, and its local disks still hold the partitions the first run read: that is the warehouse cache, in the middle of the frame. It belongs to the running warehouse, any query on it can reuse it, and it is lost when the warehouse suspends, which is the price of auto suspend. Then the step switches the result cache back on and runs the query twice more, and both are answered from the result cache, on the left, which lives in cloud services: no bytes scanned at all. Even the first, because Snowflake had stored the warm run's result while reuse was switched off; switching it on only allowed the reuse. As long as the query text is identical and the data underneath has not changed, Snowflake returns the stored result without a warehouse at all, for twenty four hours, extended each time it is reused. The third cache, on the right, is metadata: counts, minimums and maximums that cloud services keeps for every partition, which is how the very first step counted a table with no warehouse running. The table under the three shows what each run cost in this recording, read from the query history: time, bytes scanned, and time spent executing. Times vary, so read the shape, not the digits. Next, the whole map, and what this course added to it.

Here is the warehouse's map again, now with what Course 3 built lit up, and everything still to come greyed out in the place it will go. On the left, the shop database is lit: it is the one source connected so far. In the middle, inside the Snowflake account, the raw database holds its first table, and under it, W H LOAD, which costs only while it works, runs, under R M monthly's budget. The strip at the bottom names what this course made, in the order it made it: the shop's database with its four tables; the two databases, raw and analytics, with their five schemas; the products table, loaded by hand through its own stage; the warehouse, extra small and asleep after a minute; and the monitor that stops it at fifty credits a month. On the right, two honest gaps. Everything so far was done as the account's administrator, the role that can do anything, which is fine for one person on day one and wrong for a company with three teams. And only one table was loaded, by hand, from one export. A warehouse needs every source, loaded the same way every time. Those are the next two courses, in that order, because who may load data has to be settled before any data arrives. Course four gives each team a role of its own, and lets each one exactly as far as it needs to go.

So far everything has been done by Ana, the person who opened Shopwave's Snowflake account, as its administrator. A warehouse for a whole company needs more people than that, so this course decides who may do what, before any real data arrives. The first new person is Ravi, from the B I team. The editor creates his user. Notice which role creates it: user admin, the role whose job is users and roles, not the all-powerful account administrator. The terminal then asks three questions: who am I, which roles may I use, and which roles may Ravi use. Look at the side pane to see how Snowflake answers that. Privileges, such as using a warehouse or reading a table, are never granted to people. They are granted to roles, and roles are granted to users. A user can hold several roles but works as one at a time, the active role, and switches with use role. The two tables under the diagram are the run's answers. Ana can use every system role, because she created the account. Ravi has only public, the role every user gets, which by design can do almost nothing. That is the right place for a new user to start: with nothing, until a role is granted. Granting to roles rather than people is what makes a team manageable: when Ravi changes jobs, one grant changes, not fifty. Before creating roles of our own, though, we need to know the five that every account already has.

Every Snowflake account starts with the same five roles, arranged in a hierarchy, and every role higher up inherits everything granted to the roles below it. The terminal asks the account for its roles, which roles each one inherits, and which roles the account administrator holds. At the top is account admin. It can do everything, including billing and the resource monitor from the last course, which is why it should be used rarely, by few people, and never as anyone's default. Under it are two branches. On the left, security admin, which can grant any privilege on any object, and under it user admin, which creates users and roles. That branch decides who may do what. On the right, sys admin, which creates warehouses and databases, everything the warehouse is made of. That branch builds things. At the bottom is public. Every user has it automatically, so anything granted to public is granted to everyone; the rule is to grant it nothing. The custom roles this course creates next go under sys admin, so that the people who administer the account can see and manage everything the teams build. There is a sixth system role in larger companies, org admin, which manages the accounts of a whole organisation; a single trial account does not need it. With the hierarchy in mind, Shopwave can add roles of its own, one for each team.

Shopwave has three teams that touch the warehouse, so it gets three roles, one for each. The editor creates them as user admin. Loader, for the data team, which brings the sources in. Transformer, for the analytics team, which builds the models with d b t. And analyst, for B I and finance, who read the results. Each role is then granted to sys admin, as security admin. That single step is easy to forget, and it matters: a custom role that is not granted to sys admin is an orphan, and whatever it creates, the administrators cannot see or manage. Look at the side pane to see the tree that makes. Sys admin at the top inherits all three team roles, which sit side by side, none above another. Then the roles go to people. Ravi gets analyst. Ana gets all three, so that she can test each one as she builds it: she is the one setting this up. The last statement asks Snowflake who holds the analyst role, and the table in the side pane is the answer from the run: sys admin, as a role, and the two users. None of these roles can do anything yet. A role is only a name until privileges are granted to it, and that is the next step: deciding, object by object, what each team may touch.

A grant gives one privilege, on one object, to one role, and the side pane draws that shape: the privilege select and insert, on the schema raw dot Shopwave, to the role loader. The terminal first adds a warehouse, W H B I, for the analysts, so they never queue behind a load, and puts it under the same budget. Then the editor's file grants each team exactly what it needs. The loader may use its warehouse, may use the raw database, may create tables, stages, file formats and pipes in its schema, and may read and insert rows. Notice that it is done twice: on all tables, and on future tables. On all covers the tables that exist today, which is only products. On future covers every table created in that schema from now on, which is everything the next course will load. Without the future grant, tomorrow's table would be invisible to the role meant to fill it. The transformer may read raw, and may create tables and views in the three analytics schemas, which is what d b t will do in course seven. Its warehouse is created then. The analyst may use W H B I, and may read the tables and views that will appear in marts and B I, again through future grants, and nothing else. The last command asks Snowflake for the future grants on raw, and the table in the side pane is the answer. Next, all of it at once, as a matrix.

Least privilege means every role holds exactly what its job needs, and nothing more. The side pane shows the whole of the last step's file as one table: three roles across the top, the warehouses and schemas down the side, and in each cell what that role may do there. Read it by column. The loader uses its own warehouse and reads and writes raw, and that is all: it cannot see a single model. The transformer reads raw and builds in all three analytics schemas. The analyst uses the B I warehouse and reads marts and B I: it cannot see raw, and it cannot change anything. Underneath, the same thing as a flow: data moves one way, from raw, through analytics, to the marts and B I, and the privileges follow it. Each team can write only where it is responsible, and can read only what it needs. The editor asks Snowflake for its own account of two of those roles, and the terminal lists every grant each one holds, which is how you check that what was intended is what was applied. The payoff is containment. If the loader's key leaked, the damage is limited to writing into raw, which the next layer would reject in its tests, and nothing it could do reads a single customer's spending. A matrix is a promise, though, so the next step tests it, the way an analyst would, by accident.

Ravi has spotted a product with the wrong price, and as an analyst he tries to fix it where he can see it, in raw. Ana tries it first, working as the analyst role, and the first thing the terminal shows is a surprise. Her primary role is analyst, but her secondary roles are all of them: by default, Snowflake now lets a user's other roles count too, so the analyst session reads raw without complaint. Look at the side pane's top line. To act as Ravi would, the file switches secondary roles off, and then tries the update. Now Snowflake refuses, and the error is worth reading closely. It does not say permission denied. It says the database does not exist, or is not authorised. A role without access to an object cannot even learn that it is there, which is deliberate: the names of tables can themselves be sensitive. Snowflake even says which link is missing: the primary role analyst needs usage on the raw database, which it was never granted, so the update stops there. Snowflake checks every link of the chain, from the outside in. And the lesson of the first query: when testing what a role may do, test it alone, with secondary roles off. The second command, run as the administrator, finds the missing grant: it lists who holds privileges on raw, and the analyst is not among them. So should we grant it? No. The refusal is the system working. Raw holds the sources exactly as they arrived, and a wrong price is fixed where it was made, in the shop's database, and loaded again. Editing raw by hand would break the one promise raw makes. The analysts have their roles; the programs that load and transform need users of their own, which is next.

The loader and d b t are programs, not people, so they get service users, and service users never have a password. They log in with a key pair instead. The editor's script makes one for each. For the loader and for d b t, it generates a private key with open S S L and keeps it in a folder only Ana can read, then writes out the matching public key. The private key never leaves this machine, and nothing secret ever appears on screen. Then it runs the S Q L file beside it, passing the two public keys in. That file creates the two users with type service, which means they may never have a password and no person can sign in with them, gives each its public key and a default role, and grants the roles. The terminal then logs in as each of them, using only the private key, and asks Snowflake who it sees. Look at the side pane to see how a login without a password works. The client uses the private key to sign a short lived token. Snowflake checks the signature against the public key it was given, and if it matches, opens a session as that user, with its role. The table underneath is the run's answer: each service user, with its own role. A stolen password can be typed from anywhere. A key is harder to steal, but not impossible, which is what the last section of this course is about: where a login may come from.

A key can still be stolen, so Snowflake can also check where a login comes from. That is a network policy, and this frame is drawn from Snowflake's documentation rather than run, for a practical reason: a policy that allowed only Shopwave's addresses would lock out the machine this course is recorded on. On the left, two places a login can arrive from. Shopwave's loader server, at one fixed address, and anywhere else, which could be a stolen key on someone else's laptop. In the middle, the policy. It is built from a network rule, which lists the addresses that may connect in, and the policy names the rules whose addresses are allowed; everything else is blocked. It is checked before the key or the password, so a refused address never gets as far as trying one. A policy can be set on the whole account, or on a single user, and a user's own policy wins over the account's. On the right, the result. The loader's service user logs in from its server, and the same key, used from anywhere else, is refused. For Shopwave, the natural place to start is the service users, whose addresses never change, and then the whole account, once every person's network is known. That completes the account's security: roles for each team, grants that follow the data, keys for the programs, and a fence around the logins. Now the data can arrive.

Shopwave's data arrives as files: the shop database's nightly exports, the payment provider's Parquet, the website's clicks, the returns warehouse's monthly C S V. Before Snowflake can load a file, the file has to be somewhere Snowflake can read, and that place is a stage. From this course on, every load runs as the loader, so the explorer has a small script, as loader, that calls snow with the loader's own service user, its private key, its role and its warehouse. The first command creates the stage: raw dot Shopwave dot landing, an internal stage, meaning Snowflake stores the files itself, with a directory table switched on so the stage can be queried like a list. The editor's script uploads everything the generator wrote for twenty twenty six, keeping each source in its own folder. That is about ten thousand files, most of them hourly click files, so the script writes the long list of uploads to a log, prints a summary, and asks Snowflake to refresh the stage's directory. Look at the side pane to see the path a file takes. From a folder on this machine, through put, onto the stage, where it waits, still a file. Loading it into a table is a separate step, next. The table under the path is the directory table, grouped by source folder, as the run returned it: how many files landed and how big they are. A stage can also be external, pointing at a cloud bucket a sender writes to directly. Next: telling Snowflake how to read each kind of file.

Every sender writes files its own way, so before loading, Shopwave writes down how to read each kind, once, as a named file format. The editor creates four. F F C S V reads the shop's exports: comma separated, a header row to skip, text optionally in double quotes, and an empty field meaning null. F F C S V latin one is the same, but in the old Latin one encoding the returns warehouse still uses; this course's eighth section is about why that matters. F F JSON reads the site tracker's events, one JSON object per line. And F F parquet reads the payment provider's files, which carry their own column names and types. Look at the side pane to see the four as a contract: each format, what it reads, and who sends it. If a sender changes how it writes, the contract changes in one place, and every load that names it follows. The second command shows something useful about stages: you can query a staged file before loading it. It reads Black Friday's order export directly from the stage, through F F C S V, and picks out four of its columns by position, dollar one for the first, and so on. The table in the side pane is what came back: real rows, still in a file, never loaded. That is the cheapest way to check a format before trusting it with a whole year. Now the formats can be put to work.

Copy into is how a stage becomes a table. The first command creates four tables in raw dot Shopwave, with the same columns as the shop's own, plus two more on every row: the file it came from, and when it was loaded. The editor shows the load itself. For orders, copy into reads every file in the stage's orders folder, through F F C S V, and writes each file's rows into the table. Instead of loading the columns blindly, it selects them, which lets it add the file name, from a special column called metadata dollar filename, and the current time. The arrow at the end of each copy sends its result, one row per file, into a small summary query, so the terminal shows one line per table instead of one per file. Look at the side pane to see the shape of a load. Three hundred and sixty five daily files on the stage. Copy into, run by the loader's warehouse, which reads many files in parallel. And the table, with every row's source file kept. The table under it is the run's summary: how many files and rows went into orders, order items, customers and exchange rates. Keeping the file name on every row costs almost nothing and pays off the first time a number looks wrong: you can trace any row back to the exact file, and the exact day, it arrived from. A question remains, though: what happens if this load runs twice?

Loads get run twice. A schedule fires again after a failure, or someone reruns a script to be sure. So what does Snowflake do with the same copy into, run a second time? The editor runs exactly the orders load from the last section, then counts the table's rows and the distinct files they came from. The terminal shows the copy's answer: no files processed. And the count: the same orders, from the same three hundred and sixty five files, as before. Nothing was duplicated. Look at the side pane to see why. Every table keeps load metadata: for each file it has loaded, its name, its size and a checksum of its contents, kept for sixty four days. Before loading a file, copy checks that record. A file it has already loaded is skipped. So a load can safely be rerun, which is what makes a warehouse's loading dependable. The table at the bottom lists the cases where a file does load again. A file with the same name but new contents is a different file, and loads. Force equals true loads everything regardless, which duplicates rows, so it is for deliberate reloads only. And a file older than sixty four days, whose record has expired, is skipped by default, because Snowflake cannot be sure, unless you tell it to load uncertain files. Load metadata assumes the files themselves can be read, though, and the next source cannot be read so easily.

The returns arrive once a month from Shopwave's warehouse, and these files are known to be awkward. So before loading them, the step checks them. The first command creates the returns table. The editor runs copy into with validation mode set to return errors: copy reads every file and reports every row it could not load, and writes nothing at all. The summary query after the arrow groups those errors by message. Look at the side pane to see what the files contain. The twelve monthly files are read here as plain U T F eight, the format every other source uses, and they turn out to have two different problems. The first is unreadable text: every row whose return reason has an accent in it, which is a lot of them. The second is malformed rows: a few each month with a field missing or a date in the wrong format. The table in the middle is the run's count of each. They need different fixes, and that is the point of validating first: you learn which problem you have before choosing what to do. The last table is that choice. On error says what copy does when it meets a bad row: abort statement, the default, loads nothing; skip file skips that whole file; continue loads every good row and counts the bad ones, which can then be looked at. For the malformed rows, continue is right. For the unreadable text, no on error setting helps, because the problem is the encoding. We come back to that after the clicks.

The website's click events are JSON, and JSON does not fit neatly into columns: events have different fields, nested objects, and lists of items. Snowflake's answer is a column type called variant, which holds a whole JSON document. The first command creates the clicks table with a single variant column, V, plus the file and load time, and copies every click file into it, through F F JSON, one row per event. Look at the side pane to see what that means. Each JSON line becomes one variant value. Snowflake does not store it as text: it splits the document's common paths into columns internally, so querying a path is nearly as fast as querying a real column. And no schema was declared for any of it. The editor queries it with paths. V colon event type reads that field, and V colon context dot device reaches into the nested context object. Each path is then cast, with two colons, to a string, because a variant value has no type until you give it one. The query counts January's events by type and device, and the table under the diagram is the run's answer: page views, product views, adds to cart, and the rest, on mobiles, desktops and tablets. Loading JSON into a variant is the raw layer's way of keeping a source exactly as it was sent, however it changes. And on the first of June, it did.

On the first of June, the website's tracker changed what it sends. The device field moved: context dot device became context dot device type. And a new field appeared, consent, recording whether the visitor allowed tracking. Nobody told the data team. The first command asks Snowflake to infer the schema of the click files on either side of the change, the thirty first of May and the first of June, and compares the top level fields; the consent field shows up only in June. Look at the side pane to see the change on one event. On the left, May's shape; on the right, June's, with the renamed field and the new one highlighted. Because the clicks were loaded into a variant column, nothing broke: the load in the last section took both shapes without a single error. A table with a fixed column for device would have loaded June's events with that column empty, silently. The editor's query reads across both shapes. For May and June it counts, per month, how many events have the old field, how many have the new one, how many have either, using coalesce, and how many carry consent. The table in the middle is the run's answer. June has only the new field. May has the old one, except for fifteen events: clicks from the end of May that arrived late, after the switch, and were written in the new shape. Either one covers both months completely, which is why the query reads both. Notice where this is fixed. Raw keeps both shapes exactly as they were sent, and giving the device one name is staging's job, in course seven. Now the returns, and their encoding.

Back to the returns files, and the first of their two problems: text that could not be read. Look at the side pane to see why. The returns warehouse runs an old system that writes text in Latin one, an encoding where every character is one byte. In Latin one, the letter o with two dots, in the German word for size, is a single byte, F six. U T F eight, the encoding everything else uses, writes that same letter as two bytes, and a lone F six is not valid U T F eight at all. So reading these files as U T F eight fails on every row with an accent, which is what validation found. Nothing is wrong with the data. It was simply read with the wrong contract. The editor loads the returns with the right one, F F C S V latin one, which converts each byte into the right character as it loads. And it sets on error to continue, for the second problem: the few malformed rows each month are skipped and counted, while every good row loads. The second command lists the return reasons as they are now stored, in German, French and English, accents intact. Then the third command does something every load should: it reconciles. It counts the lines the warehouse was sent, reading the files with a format that ignores quotes, and the rows that loaded. Look at the table in the side pane. A hundred and eighty five rows loaded and twenty four were rejected, but seven hundred and sixty seven lines were sent. The missing hundreds are the lesson. One of the planted bad rows opens a quote it never closes, so Snowflake reads everything after it, to the end of the file, as one long broken record, and rejects it as one. Rejected counts records, not lines. On error continue made the load succeed, and quietly lost three quarters of the returns. The fix belongs to the sender, and the files are still on the stage to reload once they send it. But the warehouse's job is to notice, which is why every load is reconciled. One source is left, and it arrives every day.

The payment provider drops a Parquet file every day, and loading daily files by hand does not scale, so payments get a pipe. A pipe is a copy into statement that Snowflake runs by itself, each time a new file arrives. The editor creates the payments table, then the pipe, which loads every file in the stage's payments folder through F F parquet, matching the file's column names to the table's, so the order of columns in the file does not matter. Look at the side pane to see the flow. A file lands on the stage. The pipe is told about it, runs its copy, and the rows arrive in the payments table. A pipe does not use a warehouse at all: it runs on compute Snowflake manages, billed separately, per file, so nothing has to stay awake waiting for files. The table at the bottom answers the obvious question: how is the pipe told? With an external stage, a bucket in the cloud, the bucket itself sends an event when a file arrives, and the pipe loads it within moments: that is called auto ingest, and it needs a cloud account this course does not have, so it is cited from the documentation, not run. With an internal stage, like ours, something must ask, and alter pipe refresh does: it makes the pipe look at the folder and queue every file it has not loaded yet. The terminal refreshes, waits two minutes, and checks the pipe's state and the table's rows. Every source is now in raw. Next, the model.

Every source is now in raw, exactly as it arrived. Raw is honest, but it is shaped for the shop, not for the questions finance asks. So the warehouse needs a model built for those questions, and the most widely used way to design one comes from Ralph Kimball and Margy Ross, in The Data Warehouse Toolkit. This frame is their design process, drawn from the book, applied to Shopwave. Nothing is run here. It has four steps, in order. First, pick a business process: something the business does that produces events. For Shopwave, the first is selling: customers ordering products. Second, declare the grain: exactly what one row of the fact table means. Here, one order line, the most detailed record the shop keeps of a sale. Third, the dimensions: the ways people will slice those rows. When it happened, which customer, which product, and in what currency. Fourth, the facts: the numbers measured at that grain. The quantity, the unit price, and the amount in euros. The order matters more than anything else in the frame. The grain is chosen before any dimension or any fact, and every dimension and fact must then be true at that grain, exactly. A fact that is true per order, such as the delivery charge, does not belong on a table whose rows are order lines, because summing it would count it once per line. Choosing the grain is the one decision that is hard to undo, so it gets the next section to itself.

What does one row mean? This step answers it with one real order, number twenty two ninety three: a German customer, three lines, and, because of a glitch the data generator plants on purpose, paid twice. First the terminal creates the analytics team's own warehouse, W H transform, puts it under the budget, and lets the transformer role use it. Then, working as the transformer, it counts that one order three ways. Look at the left of the frame. At one row per order, there is one row, with the order's total, and nothing about which products were in it: too coarse to answer anything by product. At one row per order line, there are three rows, each with its product, quantity and price, and their amounts add up to the order's total: that is the grain Shopwave chooses. The third way is the trap. Join the order lines to the payments, and each line appears once per payment. This order was paid twice, so there are six rows, and the revenue doubles. The table under the three is the run's answer for each, and the doubled number sits right next to the true one. Nothing failed, no error appeared: the sum was simply wrong. That is why the rule at the bottom matters. Choose the most detailed grain the source records, and never join a fact to anything that has more than one row per key, unless you have collapsed it to one first. Next, one sales process is not the whole business.

Sales is one process. Shopwave also fulfils orders, takes returns, has visitors browsing its site, runs a checkout funnel, and wants a picture of each customer month by month. Each is a business process, and each gets a fact table of its own. The danger is building each one alone, with its own idea of what a customer or a date is, so that sales and returns can never be compared. Kimball's answer is the bus matrix, and this frame is Shopwave's, drawn as a plan, not run. Each row is a business process and the fact table that will record it, with the course that builds it. Each column is a dimension. A dot means that fact uses that dimension. Read down a column, and you see why the matrix matters: the customer dimension is shared by sales, fulfilment, returns, visits and the monthly snapshot. These are conformed dimensions: built once, used by every fact, with the same keys and the same meanings. That is what lets an analyst drill across: take revenue from sales and refunds from returns, line them up by the same customer and the same month, and trust that they mean the same things. The matrix is also a build plan. Sales comes first, in this course, with the date, customer and product dimensions. Course eight adds the currency dimension, and course nine the remaining facts, each reusing what is already there. Now, the first fact table, built by hand.

The first fact table is the one the grain decided: F C T order lines, one row per order line. In this course it is written by hand, as one create table statement, so that every part is visible; the next course rebuilds it properly with d b t. The editor shows it. It reads the order items from raw and joins each line to its order. The order id and line number identify the row. The order id has no dimension of its own, because everything about an order is already somewhere else; Kimball calls that a degenerate dimension. Then the pointers: the order date, the customer and the product, by the shop's own ids for now. Then the order's status, and the measures: quantity, unit price, and amount in euros. The comments mark which measures add up. Quantity and amount can be summed across any rows. Unit price cannot: adding two prices means nothing. Look at the side pane. This is the star, and it will stay in this shape for the rest of the course: the fact in the middle, its dimensions on either side, still empty because they do not exist yet, and the measures tinted. Under it, the check the second command ran: the fact's row count, the number of distinct order and line pairs, and the number of lines in raw. If the grain holds, all three are equal: one row per order line, none lost, none doubled. A fact with only ids is hard to read, though. It needs its dimensions.

Dimensions are what make a fact readable: they turn a product id into a name, a brand and a category. This step builds three. The editor shows the most interesting one, the date dimension, because no source sends it: the warehouse makes it. It generates one row for every day of twenty twenty six, three hundred and sixty five of them, and gives each day every attribute a report might group by: its day name, whether it falls on a weekend, its month, quarter and year, and a flag for Black Friday. A report that wants weekends versus weekdays now reads a column instead of computing it. The other two are built from raw. The customer dimension holds each customer's country, the currency they pay in, when they signed up, and their email, which course eleven will mask. The product dimension holds each product's name, brand, category and list price. Look at the side pane: the star now has three dimensions, joined to the fact's three pointers. The table underneath is the check from the last command: each dimension's row count and its number of distinct keys, which must be equal, because a dimension with two rows for one key would double every fact that joins to it, exactly the trap from the grain section. Notice the shape the frame makes. Dimensions are short and wide: a few thousand rows, many descriptive columns. Facts are long and narrow: many rows, a few keys and numbers. Next, a problem with those keys.

So far the fact points at its dimensions with the shop's own ids: a customer id, a product id. Those are natural keys, and the warehouse does not control them. This step gives every dimension a key of its own, called a surrogate key. The explorer shows the customer and product dimensions rebuilt, each with a new first column: a key made by hashing the natural key. And the editor shows the fact rebuilt to point at those keys instead: it joins to each dimension on the shop's id and keeps only the dimension's key, plus a date key, which is the date written as a number. Look at the side pane. The star's edges now run from the fact's keys to each dimension's key. The table under it says why this is worth the trouble. A natural key is made by the shop, and if the shop ever renumbers its customers, or merges two systems, every join in the warehouse breaks. A surrogate key is made by the warehouse, so it never changes underneath you. And there is a deeper reason, which arrives in course eight. When a customer moves house, the warehouse will keep both versions of that customer, and each version needs a key of its own, so one customer id can have several customer keys. The last check confirms that every fact row still finds its date, its customer and its product: no orphans. One more design choice remains before the first real answer: how far to normalise a dimension.

Look at the product dimension. Fifty products, six categories, so each category's name is stored again and again, once per product. A database designer's instinct is to normalise that: move categories into a table of their own and point to it. A dimensional model built that way is called a snowflake schema, after its shape, which has nothing to do with the product we are using. This step builds both and asks them the same question. The terminal makes a category table and a product dimension that points to it, as temporary tables that vanish when the session ends, then sums revenue by category through each model. On the left, the star: category is just a column of the product dimension, one join away from the fact. On the right, the snowflake: product points to category, two joins away. The table under the diagrams is the run's answer from both, and the numbers are the same; only the path differs. The second table is the trade. The snowflake stores each category name once, and needs an extra join for every question about categories. The star repeats the name, and in a column store that repetition costs almost nothing: a column of six distinct values compresses to almost nothing. So in a warehouse, the star wins: fewer joins, simpler queries for every analyst, and the storage it seems to waste is not really used. Shopwave keeps its star. Next, two more kinds of dimension.

Two kinds of dimension look odd at first. The first is already in the fact: the order id. It identifies the order a line belongs to, but there is no order dimension, because everything about an order, its date, customer and status, is already on the line or in another dimension. A key with no table behind it is a degenerate dimension, and it is useful: it groups lines into orders, and it is how an analyst finds a particular order. The second is a role playing dimension, and the fact gains one in this step. The fact is rebuilt with a second date key: the date the order was paid, taken from the order's first payment, so the order paid twice is still counted once. Now the fact has two dates, and both point at the same date dimension. Look at the side pane: two edges from the fact into the one date table, one solid for the order date and one dashed for the paid date. One dimension, playing two roles. The editor's query uses both roles at once, joining the date dimension twice, once as ordered and once as paid, and lists orders placed on one day but paid the next. The table under the star is the run's first five: orders placed late at night, paid after midnight. The second query counts orders with no paid date at all. Most are cancelled orders, which were never paid; the rest are the unpaid orders the generator plants, marked paid by the shop with no payment behind them. Nothing in the model stops those. Course seven turns them into a failing test. First, the question this course was built for.

In the first course, finance asked a simple question of the shop's database: revenue by category, by month. It took three joins over every line, on the server that takes the orders, and six hand written columns. This step asks the same question of the star. The editor shows the query, and it reads like the question: from the fact, join the date dimension for the month and the product dimension for the category, keep paid orders, and sum the amount. Snowflake's pivot clause then turns the six categories into six columns, which is what the shop's schema made us write by hand. The terminal shows the answer: twelve months, six categories. Look at the side pane. The star is lit along the path the query takes: the fact's date key, product key, status and amount, and the two dimensions they lead to. Under it, November, the busiest month, from both places: the shop database's answer in course one, read from that recording, and the star's answer, read from this one. They agree. That is the test of a dimensional model: it gives the same answers as the source, and it gives them from a shape built for the question, with short joins on keys, in a column store, on a warehouse of its own. But everything here was built by hand: if the data changed tomorrow, someone would have to run these scripts again, in the right order, and hope nothing broke. The next course rebuilds the star with d b t: repeatable, and tested.

The star from the last course works, but it was built by hand: a handful of scripts, run in the right order by a person who remembers the order. This course rebuilds it with d b t, a tool that turns S Q L files into a tested, repeatable build, and first, the shape that build takes. This frame is a concept, drawn from d b t's own guide to structuring a project; nothing is run. The warehouse has three layers, each built only from the one before. Raw is what course five loaded: every source exactly as it was sent, written only by the loader. Staging is one view per source table, and it does three things only: renames columns, casts types, and cleans what must be cleaned, like duplicates. It never joins two sources and never holds a business rule; it is a clean copy of the source. Marts hold the dimensional model: facts and dimensions, joined, keyed and tested, which is what the analyst role reads. The arrows between the layers are the two functions d b t gives you: source, to read raw, and ref, to read another model. The bottom of the frame names the idea behind all of it. The older way, E T L, transformed data on a separate server before loading it, so the warehouse never saw the raw data. E L T loads first and transforms inside the warehouse, in S Q L, on the warehouse's own compute: raw is always there, and any layer can be rebuilt from it. Next, a d b t project, and how it reaches Snowflake.

A d b t project is a folder of S Q L and a little configuration. The first command moves into it, the second shows the versions pinned for this course, and the third asks d b t to check that it can reach Snowflake. Three files make it a project. The explorer shows d b t project dot y m l, which names the project and says where each layer lands: staging models as views in the staging schema, marts as tables in the marts schema. A small macro beside it makes those schema names exactly staging and marts, instead of d b t's default of prefixing them. And sources dot y m l lists the eight raw tables d b t may read, so that every model refers to them by name. The editor shows the third file, profiles dot y m l: how d b t connects. Look at the side pane to follow that chain. The project names a profile. The profile says who connects: the service user S V C D B T from course four, by key pair, with the private key read from the file on this machine. Its role is the transformer, on W H transform, so everything course four granted applies: read raw, build in analytics, nothing else. Notice what is not in the profile: any secret. The account comes from an environment variable and the key from a file, so this file can be committed and shared. When d b t debug reports that every check passes and the connection is fine, the project is ready for its first models.

The first models are staging: one for each raw table. The editor shows the most interesting one, staging clicks. Its source is the clicks table from course five, where every event is a single variant column. The model turns that into typed columns: the event's id, its time, its type, the customer, and so on. The device line is where the June schema change is finally settled: coalesce takes device type where it exists, and device where it does not, so from here on every event has one device column, whatever month it is from. And the last lines remove the tracker's duplicates. The data generator sends about one event in two hundred twice, and qualify keeps exactly one row for each event id, the first one loaded. Look at the side pane. The table pairs every raw table with its staging model, as d b t's own manifest records them: orders with staging orders, clicks with staging clicks, and so on. One source, one staging model. The others are simpler than clicks: they rename columns into the warehouse's own names, like total becoming total in euros, and lower case the order status. Under the table, the three things staging clicks does, in order. The terminal runs d b t run, selecting only the staging folder, and d b t creates eight views in the staging schema, each one reported as it finishes. Views cost nothing to create, because a view stores only its query. Next, how d b t knew which order to build them in.

Nobody told d b t what order to build the models in. It works it out from the models themselves, and this step shows how. This one runs on this machine, with no connection to Snowflake at all. The terminal runs d b t parse, which reads every file in the project, finds every source and every ref, and writes a manifest: a complete description of the project. Then a short Python script reads that manifest and prints each model, how it is materialised, and the models it depends on. Everything drawn in this frame comes from that output. Look at the graph. On the left, the eight raw tables, which the staging models read with source. Next, the eight staging models. Then the marts: the customer and product dimensions, each reading one staging model; the date dimension, which reads nothing because it generates its own days; and the first payment model, which is ephemeral, more on that in a moment. And on the right, the fact, which refers to five models. This is a directed acyclic graph, a DAG: every arrow points one way, and there are no loops. Because every reference is written as ref, d b t knows that staging orders must exist before the fact, and builds everything in an order that respects every arrow, running independent models in parallel. Change one model, and d b t knows exactly which models downstream depend on it. The DAG is also what the documentation draws, at the end of this course. First, what each model actually becomes in Snowflake.

Every d b t model is a select statement. What it becomes in Snowflake is its materialisation, and this step builds the marts and looks. The editor shows the smallest model in the project, first payment: an order's earliest payment time. Its first line sets its materialisation to ephemeral. The terminal runs d b t run on the marts, then asks Snowflake's information schema what the staging and marts schemas now hold. Look at the side pane. The table at the top is the four materialisations. A view stores only the query, and computes it every time someone reads it: cheap to build, and right for staging, which is read only by the next model. A table stores the result, recomputed on every d b t run: right for marts, which many people read many times. An ephemeral model builds nothing at all: d b t pastes it into every model that refers to it, as a common table expression, which keeps small helper logic in its own file without cluttering the warehouse. And incremental, which is next. The second table is Snowflake's answer, from the run: the staging models listed as views, the dimensions and the fact as tables, and no first payment anywhere, because it was never built. That is how you check that what d b t was told is what Snowflake did. The fact, though, is rebuilt in full every run, and a year from now that will be a lot of rows to rebuild every night.

The fact table is rebuilt from scratch on every run. A year of order lines takes moments; ten years would not, and the nightly build would grow with every day of history. An incremental model rebuilds only what changed. The editor shows the fact's new first lines. Its materialisation is incremental, with a unique key, the order line key, and a merge strategy. And at the bottom, a block that applies only on incremental runs: keep only orders newer than the newest order already in the table. The terminal runs the model twice. The first run uses full refresh, which builds the whole table as if from scratch. The second is an ordinary run: d b t sees the table exists, applies the filter, and merges whatever new rows it finds, matching on the unique key, so a line that changed is updated and a new line is inserted. Look at the side pane to compare the two runs, with each run's result as d b t reported it. The full refresh created every order line. The next run had nothing newer than the newest order to merge, because no new orders have arrived since the load, so it merged nothing: that is the point. When tomorrow's orders are loaded, the next run reads only tomorrow. The cost is that the model must be correct about what is new. Orders that change after they are loaded, a status that moves from placed to paid, will not be picked up by this filter: course eight deals with that properly. Next, making sure the build is right, not just fast.

A model that builds is not a model that is right. d b t tests are how the warehouse checks itself, and the simplest are generic tests, written as a few lines of configuration. The editor shows them, in a file beside the marts. Every test is a query that should return no rows; any row it returns is a failure. The order line key must be unique and never null: that is the grain, checked on every build. The customer key and the product key must never be null, and each must have a matching row in its dimension: that is what relationships means, and it catches a fact row pointing at a customer who does not exist. The order status must be one of the three values the shop uses. And each dimension's key must be unique. Look at the side pane. The diagram shows where the tests sit on the model: the fact, checked against both dimensions. Under it, the four tests d b t ships with, and what makes each one fail. These four catch most of the mistakes a model can make: a duplicated row, a missing value, a broken join, a value nobody expected. The terminal runs d b t test on the marts, and the note at the bottom gives the result, from the run: how many passed, and how many failed. These tests check the model's structure. They do not check whether the business makes sense, and Shopwave's data has two problems no generic test can see.

Some rules belong to the business, not the model, and d b t lets you write those as custom tests: any select statement, saved in the tests folder, that returns the rows breaking the rule. The editor shows the first one. An order the shop marks as paid must have a payment: the query finds every paid order with no payment at all. The second test, beside it in the explorer, says no order is paid twice. These are the two problems the data generator plants on purpose: about one percent of orders with no payment, and a few in a thousand paid twice, the same kind as order twenty two ninety three from the grain section. The terminal runs only these two tests, and both fail. This is a failure that is meant to happen, and it is worth reading. Look at the side pane. The table is the run's result: for each test, the number of rows it found, next to what the generator planted. Under it, what a failing test means in practice. In course twelve, a failing test stops the nightly build before bad data reaches a dashboard. Then someone has to decide: is this bad data, to be fixed where it was made, in the shop or the payment provider; or a fact of life the model must handle? For double payments, Shopwave already decided, in course six: the fact takes each order's first payment, so a double payment never doubles revenue. Unpaid orders go to finance. Next, writing all of this down where everyone can find it.

The last piece of a d b t project is its documentation, and d b t writes most of it itself. The terminal runs d b t docs generate. It reads the project, as parse did, and then asks Snowflake about every model it built, its columns, types and size. Look at the side pane's table: it writes a manifest of the project, a catalog of what Snowflake holds, and a small website that combines the two, with every model's description, columns and tests, searchable, and a lineage graph. That website is normally served with d b t docs serve and opened in a browser; this course draws the same information instead, from the files themselves. The editor shows a short script that reads the manifest and prints one model's lineage: the model, then everything it reads, then everything those read, back to the sources. The terminal's last command runs it for the fact table. The diagram at the top of the side pane draws that path, read from the manifest: the raw tables, the staging models that clean them, and the fact they feed, with the dimensions beside it. Lineage answers two questions people ask every week. Where does this number come from? Follow the arrows left. And if I change this model, what breaks? Follow them right. That completes the rebuild: the same star as course six, now built by d b t from raw in the right order, tested on every run, and documented. But the star still forgets the past: when a customer moves house, every old order moves with them.

Customers change. They move house, and their loyalty tier rises as they spend. The terminal on the right shows one real customer, number eighty one, in the shop's data: signed up in Spain, then, on the sixteenth of January, moved to Austria; silver in March, gold in May. Our customer dimension has one row per customer, so what should it say? Kimball names the answers slowly changing dimensions, types zero to three, and this frame applies each to customer eighty one. Type zero never changes: the country at signup, forever, which is right for things that genuinely never change, like a date of birth, and wrong for an address. Type one overwrites: the row now says Austria. That is simple and keeps the dimension small, but history is lost, and worse, every order customer eighty one placed while living in Spain now reports as Austrian, so last year's revenue by country changes every time anyone moves. Type three keeps one step of history in an extra column, the previous country: enough for one change, not for three. Type two adds a new row for every version, each with its own surrogate key and the dates it was valid between. An order points at the version valid on the day it was placed, so it keeps its country forever, and the dimension remembers everything. This course uses type two for customers and for prices, which is exactly why course six gave every dimension a key of its own. Next, building type two with d b t.

The shop's customers table keeps only the present: when customer eighty one moved, their row was simply updated. To keep the past, the warehouse has to notice each change, and a d b t snapshot does exactly that. The first command loads the shop's change log into raw and creates customer state, a table that stands in for the shop's live customers table. The editor's script then compresses a year of nights into thirteen: once at the start of the year, before anything changed, and then at the end of each month, it sets customer state to the shop's customers as they stood that day, and runs d b t snapshot. Look at the side pane. Each time the snapshot runs, it compares customer state with what it has already recorded. For a customer whose updated at has moved, it closes the old row, setting its valid to, and adds a new row, valid from the change. Everything else is left alone. The table underneath is the snapshot's record of customer eighty one, from the run: one row per version, with the dates each was valid. There is a catch, in the note at the bottom. A snapshot can only keep what it sees. If a customer changed twice between two runs, the snapshot records one version, the second, and the first is lost for good. That is why snapshots run every night, and why, when a source keeps its own history, it is better to use that history directly, which is the next section.

Prices change too: a fifth of Shopwave's products change price during the year, some twice. But unlike customers, the shop keeps a price log: every price each product has had, and the day it started. When the source keeps its own history, there is nothing to snapshot. The warehouse can model the history directly. The first command loads the price log into raw. The editor shows the product dimension, now built from it. It joins every product to every price it has had, so a product with three prices becomes three rows, three versions, each with its own surrogate key, made from the product id and the date the price started. The window function lead looks one row ahead, at the next price's start date, and makes it this version's end: each version ends exactly where the next begins, and the current version gets an end date in the year nine nine nine nine, so that it is never in the past. Look at the side pane. The top contrasts the two sources of history: customers, where the source keeps only the present, so we snapshot it; and prices, where the source keeps a log, so we model it. The table underneath is the run's answer for products priced three ways in twenty twenty six: each version, its price, and the dates it was valid. With both dimensions versioned, the fact can now ask which version was valid when each order was placed.

Both dimensions now have versions, so the fact has to choose one, and the right one is the version valid at the moment the order was placed. The editor shows the change in the fact. The join to the customer dimension now has a second condition: the order's time must fall on or after the version's valid from, and before its valid to. The same for the product, by date. Exactly one version matches each order line, and its surrogate key is stored on the fact row for good. Look at the side pane to follow one order line through that join: placed at a moment, matched to the version valid then, and keeping that version's key. The terminal rebuilds the customer dimension and the fact with a full refresh, then asks two questions. The first lists customer eighty one's orders: the country and tier they had when they ordered, and the country they have now. The table in the side pane is the run's answer: the early orders keep their original country, the later ones say Austria, and every one of them would say Austria under type one. The second checks prices: every order line's unit price, compared with its product version's list price on the day it was ordered. The note at the bottom is the result: they match, because the shop charged the price it listed that day, and the warehouse now knows which price that was. History raises one more problem, though: some facts arrive late.

Every click event carries two dates, and usually they are the same. Look at the side pane. When it happened is the event's own time stamp, and it decides which day the click counts for. When it arrived is the day of the file it came in, and it decides when the warehouse learns about it.
