The website's tracker sometimes holds events back, so about one click in a hundred arrives up to three days late, a problem the data generator plants on purpose. The editor's query compares the two dates for every click in raw: the day it happened, against the day in its file's path, and counts the events by how many days late they were. The table in the side pane is the run's answer. Most arrive the same day; a few, one, two or three days late. A late fact must be counted in the day it happened, not the day it arrived. Staging does that already, because it uses the event's own time stamp. But it means a day's numbers can change after the day is over: Monday's sessions are not final until Thursday's files are in. Reports should say so, and incremental models must look back far enough to catch late rows, not just at today. There is a harder version, in the note at the bottom. A late fact can refer to a customer the dimension has not seen yet. Kimball's answer is an inferred member: a placeholder row for that customer, filled in when their details arrive. Next, money in four currencies.

Shopwave's prices are in euros, but its customers pay in four currencies: euros, pounds, dollars and rupees. The payments arrive in whatever currency each customer paid. And a sum of numbers in different currencies is not a number at all. This step adds the last dimension of the star, and a fact for payments. The currency dimension is small: four currencies, their names, and which one is the reporting currency, euros. The editor shows the payments fact: one row per payment, with its amount in its own currency, and the same amount in euros, divided by that day's exchange rate from the rates loaded in course five. Look at the side pane. The star now has all four dimensions, the currency dimension in its place at the bottom right, used by the payments fact. The table under it is the run's answer: payments by currency, with the amount in the currency's own units and in euros, and a total row at the bottom. Read the total row's amount column carefully: it adds pounds to rupees to dollars, and means nothing at all, even though the database computed it without complaint. The euro column's total is the only one that can be summed. That is the rule in the note, and one of the warehouse's invariants: revenue is reported in euros, through the currency dimension, and amounts in different currencies are never added together. Next, a way to see changes as they happen, inside Snowflake.

The shop's database also sends a change feed: every time an order moves on, shipped or delivered, a change record. Snowflake can track changes to a table with a stream, and this step uses one on that feed. The first command lets the loader create streams, a privilege course four did not grant. Then the editor's file, as the loader, creates the change table, and a stream on it, before any data arrives. It loads the first week of December's change files, and the summary shows how many. Look at the side pane. A stream is not a copy of the table. It is an offset: a bookmark saying how far a reader has got, and when you select from it, you see every row that changed since that bookmark, with a column saying how it changed. The file reads the stream and the first table in the side pane is the run's answer: the new rows, all inserts, counted by the status they moved to. Then it consumes the stream. Any insert, update or merge that reads from a stream, and commits, moves its offset forward to now. The file inserts the stream's rows into a table of the latest statuses, and then counts the stream again: the second table shows what was left. Nothing, because everything has been consumed. Tomorrow's load will put tomorrow's changes in the stream, and only those. That is change capture inside the warehouse, without a timestamp filter to get wrong. One more way to keep things fresh remains: dynamic tables.

Course seven kept the fact table fresh with a d b t incremental model, run on a schedule. Snowflake has its own way to do the same job: a dynamic table. The first command grants the analytics team the right to create them. The editor creates one: daily revenue, defined as an ordinary select over the fact and the date dimension, with a target lag of one hour and a warehouse to refresh it with. From then on Snowflake keeps it no more than an hour behind its sources, by itself. No schedule, no run command. How it refreshes is Snowflake's choice too: it can refresh incrementally, only what changed, or rebuild the whole table, and the run shows which it chose here: a full refresh, because, in Snowflake's own words, the query is complex, so it chose the more predictable option. An incremental refresh can be asked for when the table is created. The last statements show the dynamic table as Snowflake sees it, and then suspend it, because this is a demonstration and a dynamic table left running spends credits refreshing it. Look at the side pane to compare the two approaches. A d b t incremental model is run by a schedule, is as fresh as the last run, rebuilds what your filter says is new, and comes with tests, documentation and the lineage graph. A dynamic table is run by Snowflake, is as fresh as its target lag, decides for itself how much to rebuild, and is just the S Q L. The middle table is the run's own description of the one just made. Shopwave's choice is at the bottom. The star stays in d b t, tested every night. Small summaries that must be fresh can be either, and d b t can even build them as dynamic tables. With history in place, course nine adds every other kind of fact.

Every fact table so far has been one shape: F C T order lines, one row for each thing that happened. That is the most common shape, but it is not the only one, and some of Shopwave's questions cannot be answered by it. This frame is Kimball and Ross's answer, from The Data Warehouse Toolkit, drawn on the tables this course builds. Nothing is run here. The first column is the transaction fact. One row is one event, an order line, written when the event happens and never changed afterwards. It answers what happened. The second is the periodic snapshot. One row is a customer in a month, written for every customer at the end of every month, whether anything happened or not. Customer eighty one, the one course eight followed, gets a row for January, February and March, and so does a customer who never ordered at all. It answers how things stood at each period's end. The third is the accumulating snapshot. One row is a whole order, from placed to delivered, and unlike the other two, its row is updated: each milestone fills in as the order reaches it. The two sample rows are real orders from this course's run: one delivered two days after it was placed, one placed on New Year's Eve and not shipped yet. It answers how far each order has got, and how long each step took. Underneath, a fourth shape: a fact with no measure at all, where the row itself is the fact. Each gets a section. The accumulating snapshot comes first.

Shopwave's operations team wants to know how long orders take: from placed, to paid, to shipped, to delivered. The step starts with the rest of the year's change feed. Course eight loaded the first week of December; this load picks up every other file, and the summary shows three hundred and fifty eight files. Load metadata skips the ones already loaded. Then d b t builds two models: a staging view over the change feed, and the editor's model, F C T order lifecycle. The first block finds, for each order, the first time it was marked shipped and the first time it was marked delivered. The select then puts one order on one row: when it was placed, when it was first paid, those two dates, and a return if there was one, with the days between them as measures. Look at the side pane. The milestones, from the run: twenty thousand and twenty four orders placed, and fewer at every step after, down to the hundred and eighty five returned. An accumulating snapshot is the one fact table whose rows change. Order eighteen thousand has every date filled in; order twenty thousand and twenty, placed on the last day of the year, has nothing after paid, and the next run will fill in its dates as it moves. This one is rebuilt each run, which is simple and, at this size, cheap. The note gives the measure the table exists for: the average days from placed to delivered. The last milestone, returns, deserves its own fact.

A return undoes part of a sale, so finance wants to see returns beside the lines they undo: which products come back, why, and how much was refunded. The returns arrive from Shopwave's warehouses as a monthly C S V, loaded and checked in course five. The editor's model, F C T returns, gives each returned line its own row. The first block lists the order lines with each one's product id, taken from the product dimension. The select then joins each return to the line it undoes: the same order, and the same product. From that line it takes the keys, so a return can be sliced by customer or product exactly as a sale can, and the refund, which is the line's amount in euros. If one order held the same product twice, the last line keeps just the first match, so a return is never counted twice. Look at the side pane. The returns by reason, from the run. Every one of the hundred and eighty five found its order line: the matched column equals the returns column on every row. And the reasons are as each warehouse team typed them, in French, German and English, so the same reason appears more than once. Mapping them to one list would be a small dimension of its own. Returns came from files. The next fact comes from clicks.

The site tracker sends clicks, one row each, and marketing does not think in clicks. It thinks in visits: someone arrives, looks around, perhaps buys, and leaves. The clicks carry no visit id, so the warehouse has to find the visits itself. The usual rule, and the one used here, is a gap: if a visitor goes thirty minutes without a click, their next click starts a new session. The editor's model does it with window functions. The first block takes the staging clicks, names each visitor by customer id, or the anonymous id when they are not logged in, and uses lag to measure the minutes since that visitor's previous click. The second block marks every click that starts a session, the first one or one after a long gap, and a running sum over those marks numbers the sessions. The final select groups by visitor and session number, one row per visit, with when it started and ended, how many clicks it had, and whether it viewed a product, added to cart, checked out or bought. One line in the first block matters more than it looks: one anonymous id is excluded. Look at the side pane. The run counted the year's clicks, and that one id made about thirty thousand of them, eight percent, every one a page view. That is a scraper, not a shopper, and left in, its clicks would be counted as visits that never buy. Without it, the clicks become almost eighty thousand sessions, a little over four clicks each. Visits that view, cart and buy are a funnel.

Marketing's favourite chart is the funnel: of all the visits, how many looked at a product, how many added something to the cart, how many checked out, and how many bought. F C T funnel is the session fact grouped by day, one row per day with a count for each step, so the chart can be drawn for any week or month. The editor's first query adds up the whole year. Look at the side pane, where those numbers are drawn as the funnel. Almost every visit viewed a product. About three in five added to the cart. Then the big drop: only about a quarter of visits reached checkout. And at the end, about a quarter of all visits bought: twenty four point nine percent. But read the last two steps carefully. More visits purchased than checked out. On this site every purchase comes after a checkout, so a funnel can only narrow, and here it widens, by two. The editor's second query asks which visits bought without checking out, and the second table is its answer: three sessions, each a single click, each a purchase a minute after midnight. The rest of each of those visits, its checkout included, is not in the warehouse. The likeliest explanation is that those earlier clicks were stamped on the previous day, and that day's files never carried them. Three visits in eighty thousand changes no decision, but a funnel that widens is always a question about the data, and a check worth keeping. Funnels count events. The next fact counts the state of things at fixed times.

Finance reviews customers once a month: how many orders each placed, and which loyalty tier each was in when the month closed. That is a periodic snapshot: one row per customer per month, for every customer and every month, whether they ordered or not. The editor's model starts from the months, taken from the date dimension, and cross joins them with every customer, so a customer who did nothing in March still has a March row with zero orders. A missing row and a zero mean different things, and this table never leaves a gap. The orders block counts each customer's paid orders by month. And the tier comes from course eight's snapshot: of customer eighty one's versions, the one valid on the last day of the month. That join is the point-in-time join of course eight again, this time on a date the snapshot chose. Look at the side pane. The run counted the rows: twenty four thousand, which is two thousand customers times twelve months, exactly, the shape of the table checked by its size. Under it, customer eighty one's first six months, from the run. Two orders a month in the first quarter, then three, then five in May. Their tier moves with the snapshot: bronze, then silver at the end of March, then gold at the end of May. In June, one order, and still gold. A periodic snapshot makes questions like how many gold customers we had at each month end a simple filter. But summing its columns needs care, and that is the next section.

A fact table's numbers are not all the same kind, and a dashboard that sums the wrong one gives a confident wrong answer. The side pane's first table names the three kinds. Additive measures, like revenue and quantity, can be summed across any dimension. Semi additive measures, like how many customers were gold at a month end, can be summed across customers, but not across time. Non additive measures, like average order value, cannot be summed at all. The editor's file tests the last two against the warehouse. The first query computes A O V twice. The right way: total revenue divided by total orders. The tempting way: work out each customer's own average order value, and average those. The second table in the side pane is the run's answer, and the two disagree by about eight euros. The averaged version gives every customer the same weight, so a customer with one expensive order counts as much as one with twenty ordinary orders. A ratio has to be rebuilt from its parts, the sums, at whatever level it is shown. The second query uses the monthly snapshot from the last section. Counting gold customers at the end of December gives a hundred and thirty four. Adding up the gold customers of all twelve month ends gives six hundred and twenty four, which counts the same customers again and again, once for every month they stayed gold. Across time, a semi additive measure takes the last value, or an average, never a sum. One kind of fact remains: one with no measure at all.

Marketing ran four campaigns in twenty twenty six, and the question it asks is not only who bought through each one. It is also who could have, and did not. A sales fact cannot answer that, because it only holds what happened. What is needed is a table of what could have happened, and Kimball calls it a factless fact: a row with no measure, where the row itself is the fact. The step loads the campaign calendar first: one J S O N file, an array of four campaigns, each with its start and end date. The loader's status line shows the four rows loaded. Then the editor's model, F C T eligibility. It says a customer was eligible for a campaign if they visited the site while it ran, taking the visits from the session fact. The result is one row per campaign and customer, and nothing else: no amount, no count. Look at the side pane. The query counts, for each campaign, the eligible customers, and how many of them had a visit through that campaign that ended in a purchase. The last column is the difference, and it is the column this table exists for. The newsletter reached all two thousand customers, and a little under two thirds bought through it. Black Friday reached fewer, and only about one in nine of them bought through it, though every one of the rest visited while it ran. A count of what did not happen can only come from a table of what could have. That completes the facts. The warehouse is now complete enough to be slow, and the next course makes it fast and cheap.

The warehouse now answers every question finance and marketing have asked. The next question is how fast, and at what cost. Before changing anything, look at how Snowflake actually runs a query. This frame is the dashboard's main query: November's revenue by day and by product category, from the order lines joined to the date and product dimensions. Snowsight draws a query profile as a picture; the same information is available as rows, from a function called get query operator stats, and that is what this step read, straight after running the query. Each box is one operator from the run, with the rows it passed on and its share of the time. Read each column from the top. On the left, the order lines are scanned, then filtered, then partly aggregated. In the middle, the date dimension is scanned and filtered down to thirty rows, the days of November, and joined to the order lines. On the right, the sixty six product versions are scanned, joined in, and the rows are aggregated by day and category, sorted, and returned. The operator marked in red is where nearly all the time went: reading the order lines. That is normal. In a warehouse the expensive part of a query is almost always reading data, so making a query fast mostly means reading less of it. There is a hint of that in the profile already: the operator called join filter. Snowflake used the dates the join needed to skip some order lines before they reached the join. How Snowflake avoids reading data is called pruning, and it is next.

Snowflake stores a table as micro partitions, and for every partition it keeps a little metadata, including the smallest and largest value of every column. When a query filters on a column, Snowflake compares the filter with each partition's range first, and a partition whose range cannot contain a match is never read. That is pruning, and it is the side pane's first diagram. The editor's file measures it on the order lines. The first query asks Snowflake how the table is laid out by order date. The second table in the side pane is its answer: eight partitions, each one overlapping all seven others, and a depth of eight. Depth is how many partitions a single date could be in, so eight means any date might be in any partition. Even a table this small is written as eight partitions, by the eight threads of an extra small warehouse working side by side. The second query sums November's orders, and the third asks the query profile how many partitions the scan read: eight of eight. Nothing was skipped. Every partition holds orders from the whole year, because the table was written in whatever order the join produced them, so every partition's range includes November. The filter was correct, the answer was correct, and Snowflake still had to read the whole table. On a table this size that costs nothing worth measuring. On a table of years, with thousands of partitions, it is the difference between reading a month and reading everything. The fix is to control how the rows are laid out, with a clustering key.

If rows from the same month were stored together, a query for one month could skip most of the table. A clustering key tells Snowflake which column to keep rows together by. Here the change is one line in the model's config: cluster by order date key. When d b t builds a table with a clustering key, it sorts the rows by that key as it writes them, and it declares the key on the table. The first command rebuilds the order lines from scratch, with full refresh, so the whole table is written in the new order. Then the same two questions as last time. The side pane puts the two runs side by side. Before: eight partitions, each overlapping seven others, with a depth of eight. After: still eight partitions, but none of them overlap, and the depth is one. Each partition now holds one stretch of the year, so its smallest and largest dates are close together. And the November query read two partitions of the eight, not all of them. The answer, three hundred and twenty two thousand euros, is the same, because pruning never changes a result, only how much is read to get it. There is a cost, and the note names it. A table with a clustering key gets automatic clustering: as new orders are merged in each night, the table drifts out of order, and Snowflake re sorts it in the background, with its own compute, billed separately. For a table queried by date all day, that is usually worth it. For a small table, or one rarely filtered, it is not. Reading less is one lever. The other is how much compute does the reading.

A warehouse can be made faster in two different ways, and they solve different problems. The side pane's first diagram sets them side by side. Scaling up means a bigger size. Each size up doubles the compute and doubles the credits per hour, and it helps one heavy job, like d b t's biggest models, finish sooner. Scaling out means more clusters of the same size. It does not make any single query faster, but it lets more queries run at the same moment, which is what a dashboard needs when everyone opens it at once. The first two commands, as an administrator, do both. The analytics team's warehouse goes from extra small to small, and the B I warehouse may now run up to three clusters, with the standard scaling policy. The second table shows the warehouses afterwards, from the run. Then the editor's script plays Black Friday morning. It connects as an analyst on the B I warehouse and sends the dashboard query ninety six times, without waiting for any of them to finish, so they all arrive together. When they are done, it asks the warehouse's own history which cluster ran each query, and how long the longest one waited in a queue. The third table is the answer. Snowflake started a second cluster when the queries began to queue, and that cluster took a few of them; no query waited long enough to show. That is scaling out doing its job. Compute is one way to answer faster. Storing the answer in advance is another.

Some questions are asked so often that it is worth storing the answer. The first statement in the editor creates a materialised view: daily revenue from the paid order lines, one row a day. Unlike an ordinary view, its result is stored, and Snowflake keeps it up to date by itself whenever the order lines change. The file then asks for November's revenue twice, once from the order lines and once from the view, and after each, it reads the query profile. The side pane's second table compares them, from the run. The order lines query scanned four thousand one hundred and seventy five rows to add them up. The view query read thirty rows, one per day of November, with an operator called materialized view scan. The same answer, from more than a hundred times fewer rows. The bottom of the file looks at a second feature, search optimisation, which builds an index like structure so that looking up a single value, such as one order id, can skip almost every partition. It is not switched on here. Instead, Snowflake's own estimate function says what it would cost on this table, and the third table shows the estimate: a tiny build cost in credits, storage too small to show, and no maintenance figure yet. On a table this small it would not be worth anything, and on a large table looked up by id it often is. Both features have the same catch, which the note spells out: they are maintained in the background, on credits you do not see in a warehouse. The view was a measurement, so the last statement drops it. Next, a feature for the queries that do not fit.

Most queries a dashboard runs are small. But now and then someone runs one huge scan, and sizing the whole warehouse up for that one query means paying the bigger size every hour it runs. The query acceleration service is Snowflake's answer, and the side pane's diagram shows the idea. The warehouse runs the query as usual, but parts of a big scan can be handed to a pool of shared compute, many servers for a few seconds, up to a limit set as a scale factor of the warehouse. It is billed only for the seconds it is used. Not every query can use it, so before switching it on, Snowflake will estimate, for any query that has already run, whether acceleration would have helped. The editor's file runs the kind of query that might qualify: every click of the year, read from the raw table and counted by campaign. The first table in the terminal is its answer. Most clicks came with no campaign at all, and the newsletter and retargeting brought in about fifty thousand each. Then the file asks for the estimate for that query, and the side pane shows the result: ineligible, with a scale factor of zero. That is the honest answer for this warehouse. According to Snowflake's documentation, acceleration helps scans of many partitions that dominate a query's time, and a year of clicks here fits in eight partitions, too few to split up. So it stays switched off. On a large table, the same estimate is the right first step, run before paying for anything. All of this has been about spending less. The last section finds out where the credits actually go.

Every night d b t rebuilds the warehouse, and the bill for that arrives as credits on one warehouse. Which models are expensive? Snowflake cannot tell you directly, because it does not know what a model is. But every query can carry a label, called a query tag, and the editor's macro makes d b t set the tag to the model's name before it runs each model's queries. This is a pattern from d b t's own Snowflake documentation: a macro named set query tag replaces the built in one, and every model picks it up without a change. The first command runs the whole project, all twenty two models, on the analytics warehouse, now a small. Then the file reads that warehouse's query history from the last ten minutes, groups the queries by tag, and adds up their execution time. The side pane's table is the answer, from the run: the six models that took the most time, how many queries each ran, and each one's share of the total. No model dominates; the time is spread across the date dimension, the sessions, the lifecycle, the payments and the rest. That is what a warehouse this small looks like, and it is also what a healthy one looks like. The note explains why this is time and not credits. A warehouse is billed for every second it is running, with a minimum of a minute each time it resumes, not per query. So the fair way to split a run's bill is by each model's share of the time. When one model starts taking half, this query is how you will notice. The warehouse is fast and its costs are known. The next course serves it to its readers.

The star answers any question, but a dashboard asks the same few questions all day, and it should not have to know how the star fits together. So the last layer is a mart built for the dashboard, in its own schema, B I. The editor's model is the first: mart revenue. It joins the order lines to the date and the product dimensions, keeps paid orders only, and collapses everything to one row per day and category: how many orders, the revenue in euros, and the average order value. d b t builds it as a table of a little over two thousand rows, one for each day and category that had sales. The side pane's diagram is the whole idea: the dashboard reads the mart, never the star, so the star can change shape without breaking a chart. The query then reads Black Friday week back from the mart, and the table shows it, day by day. Most days bring in four or five thousand euros. Black Friday, the twenty seventh of November, brings in ninety eight thousand: about twenty times an ordinary day, the spike the data generator was told to plant, now visible in one row of a mart. One caution is written under it. The orders and average order value columns are per category, so an order that bought a book and a lipstick counts once in books and once in beauty. A day's orders are not the sum of its rows, which is the non additive measure from course nine again. The revenue column, though, adds up safely. Revenue is one question; whether customers come back is another.

A shop lives on customers who come back, and the standard way to measure that is a cohort table. A cohort is a group of customers who started together, here the month of each customer's first paid order. The editor's model, mart cohorts, works it out in three steps, the side pane's diagram. The first block lists which months each customer ordered in. The second finds each customer's first month, their cohort. The third counts each cohort's size. The final select then counts, for every cohort and every month after it, how many of its customers ordered again, and divides by the cohort's size. The query pivots the first six cohorts into the triangle in the side pane, from the run. Each row is a cohort, with its size, and each column is a number of months later. January's cohort is large, nine hundred and five customers, and the note explains why it is not a true cohort: the data starts on the first of January, so every customer who already existed makes their first order of the year in January, and joins it. From February on, the cohorts are real: three hundred and fifty six new customers, then fewer each month, because there are fewer customers left who have never ordered. Read along a row: in this data, between about thirty and fifty percent of a cohort order again in each later month, and the rows barely fade. Real cohorts usually fall away faster, and that difference is exactly what a retention chart is for. Before more marts, there is a problem to fix: Shopwave has more than one idea of revenue.

Ask three teams for November's revenue and Shopwave would get three answers. This course already printed two of them. Course ten summed every order line in November; later, it summed paid orders only. The finance team, meanwhile, subtracts refunds. None of them is wrong; they answer different questions under the same name, and that is how a board meeting ends up arguing about numbers instead of decisions. The fix is to define revenue once, in one model, and have every report read it. The side pane's diagram is the definition: paid orders only, in euros, using the order lines' own euro prices so no currencies are ever mixed, and net of what was refunded on those orders, taken from the returns fact of course nine. The editor's model, metrics monthly, implements it: sales by month, refunds joined back to the lines they undo, and the net. The first query puts the three answers for November side by side, from the run. Every order line: three hundred and twenty two thousand euros. Paid orders only: two hundred and eighty eight thousand. Paid, net of refunds: two hundred and eighty six thousand seven hundred. The gaps are explained, line by line: thirty five thousand euros of orders that were never paid, and about twelve hundred euros refunded. The last table is the metric month by month, and November stands out, Black Friday again. From now on, revenue means this table. The rest of this course is about who may see what, starting with the customers' emails.

The customer dimension holds email addresses, which are personal data. The analysts need customers, but not their emails, and the rule should hold whatever tool they use. Snowflake's answer is a masking policy: a small function attached to a column, which Snowflake applies to every query, before the result leaves. The first command lets the analytics team create masking policies in the marts. The editor's file creates the policy, P I I email: if the role a session is working as is the transformer, the email comes back as it is; for anyone else, the name is replaced with stars and only the domain is left, which is still enough to count customers by email provider. The policy checks current role on purpose. Ana holds every role, so her secondary roles always include the transformer, and the note explains it: the policy answers to the one role she is working as, not every role she could use. Then d b t rebuilds the customer dimension, and there is a catch, the first note. d b t replaces the table on every run, and a replaced table loses its policies. So the model attaches the policy itself, in a post hook, every time it builds. The last file reads customer eighty one twice. As the transformer, the side pane's table shows the real address. Then the same session switches to the analyst role, alone, as course four taught, and the same query returns stars and the domain. One column, two readers, one rule. Masking hides values. The next policy hides whole rows.

Shopwave has country managers, and the German manager should see German customers, not French ones. That is not a different table for each country; it is the same table, filtered by who is asking, and Snowflake does it with a row access policy. The first command creates the role, region manager, with everything an analyst can read, and lets the analytics team create row access policies. The editor's file starts with a small mapping table, region countries, which says which countries each role may see. Here, region manager sees Germany and Austria. Keeping this as data matters: a manager for France would be one more row, not a new policy. Then the policy, by region. It returns true, meaning the row is visible, if the session is working as the transformer or the analyst, or if the mapping table pairs the session's role with the row's country. d b t rebuilds the customer dimension, and the model's post hook now attaches both policies. The query counts customers by country twice, and the side pane shows both answers, from the run. As the transformer: Germany, then France, Britain and Italy, the whole table. As the region manager, with nothing else switched on: Germany and Austria, and nothing else. No error, no warning, the other rows simply do not exist for that role. Notice Austria has sixty eight customers: customer eighty one, who moved there from Spain, is among them, through the customer's second version. Next, a view that hides not rows, but how it is built.

Brightline, the marketing agency, wants to see how its campaigns perform. Shopwave wants to show it that and nothing more: not the sessions table, not the customers, and not even how the numbers are worked out. The tool for that is a secure view. The editor's model is an ordinary d b t view with two settings in its config. Secure true makes it a secure view. Copy grants true means that when d b t replaces the view, it keeps the grants already on it, which will matter in the next section. The view itself is simple: visits and buying visits per campaign and week, from the session fact, with each campaign's channel. The side pane's diagram lists what a secure view hides. The rows are shown to anyone allowed to select them. The definition is hidden: the S Q L, and the tables behind it. And Snowflake's optimiser is not allowed shortcuts that could reveal rows the view filters out, which can make a secure view slower than an ordinary one. The query file tests it as an analyst. The analyst reads the view, and the second table shows the campaigns, from the run: the newsletter and retargeting each brought over eleven thousand visits. Then the file asks Snowflake to show the view, including its text, and the third table compares the two readers: for the analyst the text is empty, for the transformer, who owns it, the definition is there. Only a secure view can be shared with another Snowflake account, and that is the next step: giving it to Brightline.

Shopwave could export the campaign numbers to a file every week and email it to Brightline. Snowflake offers something better: a share. A share is a set of grants on objects, given to another account, which then reads them in place. Nothing is copied, so Brightline always sees today's numbers. The side pane's diagram is the path. The first command, as an administrator, creates the share, shopwave campaigns, and grants it the database, the B I schema, and select on the secure view, and nothing else. Brightline has no Snowflake account of its own, so the second script creates one for it: a reader account. Shopwave owns it and pays for its compute, and it can only read what is shared with it. The script keeps the generated admin password in a key file, never on screen, adds the reader account to the share, and shows the share going out, the first table in the side pane. The third command runs inside Brightline's account. The editor's file creates a small warehouse there, which Shopwave pays for, mounts the share as a database, and reads the campaign view. The second table is Brightline's answer, from inside its own account, and it matches what the analyst saw in the last section, row for row. Finally the file tries to read the sessions table through the same database, and is refused: that schema does not exist for Brightline. Only what was granted to the share crosses over. Everything is now in place for the dashboard.

The course began with a question from Shopwave's management: how much did Black Friday bring in, and from which categories? Here is that question, answered the way the dashboard answers it. The map at the top now has its serving layer lit: the revenue mart and the metrics, the policies, the dashboard, and the share to Brightline. Under it, the side pane's first diagram is what a single dashboard tile actually reads. It reads the revenue mart, which uses the one definition of revenue. It runs on the B I warehouse, which can add clusters when everyone opens the dashboard at once. And it runs as the analyst, so customer emails stay masked. The dashboard tool itself is not shown: it is just one more client sending this S Q L, and this step ran the same query as an analyst. The table on the right is the tile's content, from the run. Electronics brought in the most, thirty one thousand euros, from two hundred and eighty seven orders. Beauty came close behind with far more orders, four hundred and thirty seven, at a much lower average. Then sports, home and fashion, and books last, with the smallest average order of all. The note gives the total: ninety eight thousand euros of paid orders on one day. That number has passed through every course: loaded from files, modelled into a star, tested by d b t, kept in history, clustered for speed, and defined once. The warehouse is built and serving. The last course keeps it running, every night, safely.
